[Migrating from Testing Library | Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/testing-library)\n\n# Playwright Component Testing for React\n\nPlaywright offers experimental component testing capabilities for React applications.[1][3] Here's what you need to know:\n\n## Getting Started\n\nInstallation is straightforward using the command:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nnpm init playwright@latest -- --ct\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis creates necessary configuration files including a &#96;playwright/index.html&#96; file (with a root div for mounting components) and test files.[1][3]\n\n## Basic Test Structure\n\nA typical component test looks like this:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';\nimport App from './App';\n\ntest('should work', async ({ mount }) =\u003e {\n  const component = await mount(\u003cApp /\u003e);\n  await expect(component).toContainText('Learn React');\n});\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRun tests with &#96;npm run test-ct&#96;.[1][3]\n\n## Key Advantages\n\nTests run in Node.js while components run in a real browser, combining the benefits of both environments.[1][3] This enables real clicks, actual layout execution, and visual regression testing while leveraging Node.js capabilities and Playwright features like parallel testing and tracing.[1][3]\n\n## Important Limitations\n\n- You can only pass plain JavaScript objects and built-in types (strings, numbers, dates) to components—not complex Node.js objects[1][3]\n- You cannot pass data synchronously through callbacks, as the callback lives in Node while the component runs in the browser[1][3]\n\n## Migration from Testing Library\n\nPlaywright provides migration guidance from React Testing Library, with equivalent APIs (e.g., &#96;render()&#96; → &#96;mount()&#96;, &#96;screen&#96; → &#96;component&#96;).[4][5]",

## Bottom Line
For your current repo, most of this list falls into 3 buckets:

- Keep using what already matches your stack: `Next.js`, `TypeScript`, `Tailwind`, `Drizzle`, `ESLint`, `Vitest`, `Playwright`, `pnpm`, `PostCSS`, `tsx`, `Node.js`, `SWC`.
- Add a small number of high-value tools soon: `Knip`, `CSpell`, `MSW`, `Sentry`, `size-limit`, and maybe `SVGO`/`SVGR`.
- Skip the rest unless your roadmap changes, because many are competing frameworks, alternate bundlers, alternate ORMs, or release/monorepo tooling you do not need for a single Next.js 16 app with its own CMS.

## Best Candidates For Your Project
If I had to shortlist the most useful additions for this specific repo, I’d pick these:

- `Knip`: best cleanup tool for unused files, exports, and dependencies.
- `CSpell`: catches bad spelling in UI text, docs, and code identifiers with very low maintenance cost.
- `Mock Service Worker`: best next testing upgrade for realistic API mocking in `Vitest` and `Playwright`.
- `Sentry`: best production monitoring upgrade once the site/admin are live.
- `size-limit`: very relevant for a public portfolio where bundle weight matters.
- `SVGO`: useful if you keep raw SVG assets.
- `SVGR`: useful if you often turn SVGs into React components.
- `simple-git-hooks` or `husky` + `lint-staged` + `commitlint`: worth it if you want stricter repo hygiene.
- `next-intl`: only if you plan multilingual content.
- `MDX` / `Next.js MDX` / `Remark`: only if you want blog posts, case studies, or richer content pages.
- `dependency-cruiser`: useful later if you want to enforce boundaries between `app`, `components`, `lib`, and admin/public areas.
- `Vercel OG`: strong fit if you want dynamic Open Graph images.

## Curated Report

- `CSpell`: `Use now`. Low-cost quality boost for UI copy, docs, and code spelling.

- `GitHub Actions`: `Use`. Same verdict as above; very relevant for this repo.
- `Mock Service Worker`: `Use soon`. Best companion to `Vitest` and `Playwright` for realistic API mocking.

- `Node.js`: `Keep`. Core runtime for Next, tooling, and CI.

Yes. A few important `Next.js 16`-relevant tools were missing from your list.

## Most Useful Missing Tools
- `@next/bundle-analyzer`
  Best missing tool for your repo. It helps you inspect client/server bundles and is very useful in a portfolio site where bundle size matters.

- `@vercel/analytics`
  Good if you deploy on Vercel and want lightweight traffic/event analytics without adding a heavier analytics stack.

- `@vercel/speed-insights`
  Very relevant for `Next.js` because it gives real Core Web Vitals and route performance data in production.

- `zod`
  This is the big one. For a `Next.js` app with forms, server actions, auth, and DB writes, `zod` is one of the most useful missing tools on the whole list.

- `next-safe-action`
  Strong fit if you lean on Server Actions. It adds typed input validation, safer execution, and cleaner action patterns on top of native Next actions.

- `react-scan`
  Very useful in development to catch unnecessary re-renders and React performance issues, especially in interactive dashboard/admin UI.

- `@axe-core/playwright`
  Excellent if you keep `Playwright`. It gives automated accessibility checks inside E2E tests and fits your public site well.

## Good Missing Tools, But More Optional
- `@vercel/og`
  You listed `Vercel OG`, which is good. If you meant the actual package/tooling layer, this is still worth calling out as a real implementation choice for dynamic OG images.

- `@next/mdx`
  You listed `MDX` and `Next.js MDX`, but the official integration package itself is worth explicitly knowing because that is what you would actually wire into the app.

- `react-hook-form`
  Not mandatory in React 19 + Server Actions, but still very useful if your admin dashboard gets larger, more dynamic forms.

- `axe-core` / `jest-axe` / `vitest-axe`
  Good companions if you want accessibility checks at unit/integration level, not only in browser E2E.

## Things I Would Not Add Despite Being Popular
- `next-seo`
  I would not treat this as a missing tool. In App Router, Next’s native metadata API already covers most SEO work better.

- `Prettier` if you move to `Biome`
  Pick one formatter direction, not both.

- `TanStack Query`
  Only add it if you have a lot of client-side async state, optimistic updates, or repeated client fetching. For a server-first `Next.js 16` app, it is not automatically needed.

## My Real Priority Order For Your Project
1. `zod`
2. `@next/bundle-analyzer`
3. `@vercel/speed-insights`
4. `@vercel/analytics`
5. `next-safe-action`
6. `@axe-core/playwright`
7. `react-scan`

Here is what was set up and why.

## What changed

1. **`husky` (^9.1.7)**  
   - Added as a devDependency and wired so installs register Git hooks via the [`prepare` script](https://typicode.github.io/husky/) (recommended for npm/pnpm).

2. **`package.json`**  
   - `"prepare": "husky"` — runs after `pnpm install` so clones get `core.hooksPath` set to `.husky/_`.

3. **`.husky/pre-commit`**  
   - `husky init` had set this to `pnpm test`, which would run **Vitest** on every commit (and your `test` script is the watch-style entry, so it is a poor default).  
   - Replaced with a **no-op** (`:`) plus short comments so commits are not blocked until you add lint-staged / lint / etc.

4. **Verified**  
   - `git config core.hooksPath` → `.husky/_`  
   - `pnpm prepare` runs cleanly  
   - `.husky/pre-commit` exits `0`

## Files to know

| Path | Role |
|------|------|
| `package.json` | `"prepare": "husky"` |
| `.husky/pre-commit` | Your extension point for future steps (pnpm scripts) |
| `.husky/_/` | Husky’s dispatcher (do not delete; [Husky docs](https://typicode.github.io/husky/)) |

## Optional: skip hooks once

```bash
HUSKY=0 git commit -m "message"
```

When you’re ready for the next step, we can add **lint-staged** and chain `pnpm lint`, `pnpm test -- run`, spellcheck, etc., inside this same `pre-commit` file or via a small script.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
No "type": "module" means CommonJS is used by default for . lint-staged supports configuration via `lint-staged.config.js` or the `lint-staged` field in `package.json`. I'll use the `lint-staged` field in `package.json` for simplicity, though complex globs are cleaner in a dedicated file. lint-staged v15 allows exporting default from `lint-staged.config.mjs`.

Globs order matters in lint-staged - more specific patterns should come first. Each pattern runs independently for matching files. For overlaps: a file matching multiple patterns runs multiple times - we should avoid this. Typically:
- One pattern for `*.{js,jsx,...` lint-staged should prioritize specific patterns, running each pattern independently without overlap. For example:
- Use `*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}` for ESLint and Prettier formatting
- Use `*.{json,md}` for Prettier only, avoiding unintended formatting of `package.json` and `package-lock.json`

Prettier respects `.prettierignore`, so it's safe to explicitly exclude `package-lock.json` and other lock files. Markdown files like `README.md` and documentation can be formatted using Prettier. YAML files in `.github/workflows` can also be included. While including all files (`*`) may seem convenient, it's risky and should be avoided in favor of explicit extensions. lint-staged supports various extensions, including js, jsx, ts, tsx, json, md, yaml, and html. For this repository, two main globs are configured:

- `*.{js,jsx,mjs,cjs,ts,tsx,mts,cts}`: Runs ESLint fix and Prettier write
- `*.{json,md,mdx,css,scss,html,yml,yaml}`: Runs Prettier write only

This setup avoids overlap by prioritizing specific patterns and excludes lock files and package.json from unintended formatting. Shell scripts (.sh) are not formatted by default with Prettier.

To run lint-staged manually, add the script `"lint-staged": "lint-staged"` to package.json. To update pre-commit, run `pnpm exec lint-staged` or `pnpm lint-staged`. Husky recommends using `pnpm lint-staged` with the script added to package.json.

- Add `"lint-staged": "lint-staged"` to scripts in package.json
- Use `pnpm exec lint-staged` for cross-platform compatibility
- lint-staged runs tasks concurrently by default in v13+, but sequential execution is needed for same-file operations (e.g., eslint followed by prettier)
- For pre-commit hooks, use `pnpm exec lint-staged` in shell scripts Remove old comments or merge with new short comment.

Husky pre-commit doesn't require a shebang in v9 samples  `sh` is used instead.

ESLint on Windows with special character paths  lint-staged handles this automatically.

Here’s what was added and how it behaves.

## What was set up

1. **`lint-staged` (^16.4.0)**  
   - Dev dependency, as in the [lint-staged package docs](https://www.npmjs.com/package/lint-staged).

2. **`lint-staged.config.mjs`**  
   - **TS/JS (`*.{js,jsx,mjs,cjs,ts,tsx,mts,cts}`):** `eslint --fix`, then `prettier --write` (Prettier last, consistent with `eslint-config-prettier`).  
   - **Other formatted files:** `*.{json,md,mdx,css,scss,html,yml,yaml}` → `prettier --write` only.  
   - **Not** wired here: `cspell`, `knip`, full `tsc`, or `vitest` — they’re heavier or whole-repo; keep them for `pnpm`/CI.

3. **`package.json`**  
   - `"lint:staged": "lint-staged"` so you can run the same thing as the hook: `pnpm run lint:staged`.

4. **`.husky/pre-commit`**  
   - Calls `pnpm run lint:staged` instead of a no-op.

## How to try it

```bash
git add path/to/file.tsx
pnpm run lint:staged   # or commit — hook runs the same
```

With nothing staged, lint-staged exits successfully (you should see that it found no staged files).

## Skipping the hook (one-off)

```bash
HUSKY=0 git commit -m "…"
```

If you want **warnings to fail the commit** as well, we can add `eslint --max-warnings=0` only for the lint-staged TS/JS step (your global `pnpm lint` can stay as-is).

A regex pattern `/^Merge /.test(message)` can be used to identify these messages, though it may be too broad. Additional patterns like "Squashed commit of the following:" from GitHub squash merges might also need to be ignored. ## Your commits

Recent messages already look like **[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `build:`, `docs:`, `perf:`). One older line used **`feat & style:`**, which is **not** valid conventional (type must be a single token). **`@commitlint/config-conventional`** will reject that style going forward; use something like `style:` or `feat:` (or split into two commits).

## What was set up

| Piece | Purpose |
|--------|--------|
| `@commitlint/cli` + `@commitlint/config-conventional` | CLI + [conventional preset](https://commitlint.js.org/guides/getting-started.html) |
| `commitlint.config.mjs` | ESM config (recommended with **Node 24** so commitlint can load the file reliably, per [getting started](https://commitlint.js.org/guides/getting-started.html)) |
| `.husky/commit-msg` | Runs `commitlint --edit "$1"` on the message file |
| `"commitlint": "commitlint"` in `package.json` | Lets you run `pnpm commitlint` manually |

**Merge / revert:** Ignores messages that start with `Merge` or `Revert` so normal Git merge/revert commits are not blocked.

```bash

```

Yes. **`commitlint.config.mts` is supported.**

`@commitlint/load` looks for that filename and loads `.mts` with the same TypeScript loader as `.ts` / `.cts` (see [`load-config.ts` in commitlint](https://github.com/conventional-changelog/commitlint/blob/master/%40commitlint/load/src/utils/load-config.ts): `commitlint.config.mts` is in `searchPlaces`, and `.mts` uses `TypeScriptLoader`).

The old [getting started](https://commitlint.js.org/guides/getting-started.html) note about **`.mjs`** was mainly for **Node 24 + CJS/ESM edge cases** when the config was **`commitlint.config.js`**. Using **`.mts`** avoids that and matches the rest of your typed config style.

I replaced `commitlint.config.mjs` with **`commitlint.config.mts`**, typed with `UserConfig` from `@commitlint/types`, and checked that `echo "feat: test" | pnpm exec commitlint` still passes.

## How Husky works (in your repo)

1. **`package.json` has `"prepare": "husky"`**  
   After `pnpm install`, `prepare` runs and Husky wires Git to use a **custom hooks directory** instead of the default `.git/hooks/`.  
   That directory is **`core.hooksPath` → `.husky/_`** (you can confirm with `git config core.hooksPath`).

2. **What Git actually runs**  
   For each event (e.g. `pre-commit`, `commit-msg`), Git runs a **small script under `.husky/_/`** that delegates to Husky’s dispatcher (`h`), which then runs **your script** in `.husky/<hook-name>` if it exists.

3. **Your scripts are the “real” hooks**  
   - **`.husky/pre-commit`** — runs when you `git commit`, **before** the commit is created. Yours runs `pnpm run lint-staged`.  
   - **`.husky/commit-msg`** — runs **after** the message is written but **before** the commit is finalized. Yours runs `commitlint` on the message file.

So Husky is **not** magic: it’s a thin layer that (1) installs the Git hook wiring once, and (2) keeps hook scripts in `.husky/` so they can be committed and shared.

---

## What `.husky/commit-msg` is

**`commit-msg` is a standard Git hook.** Git calls it with **one argument**: the **path to a temporary file** that contains the commit message (subject + body).

Your file does:

```sh
pnpm exec commitlint --edit "$1"
```

- **`$1`** is that path (e.g. `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG` or a temp file).  
- **`commitlint --edit <file>`** reads the message from that file and exits non‑zero if it breaks your rules.

So **`.husky/commit-msg` = “whenever someone commits, lint the message file with commitlint.”**  
It does **not** run on `git push` or merges by default in the same way; it runs when Git is validating the **commit message** for a new commit (including `git commit`, and some amend flows).

---

## Order vs `pre-commit`

| Hook           | When                         | Your use        |
|----------------|------------------------------|-----------------|
| `pre-commit`   | Before commit is recorded    | lint-staged     |
| `commit-msg`   | Message is fixed; commit not finalized yet | commitlint |

If `pre-commit` fails, you never get to `commit-msg`. If `pre-commit` passes but the message is bad, `commit-msg` fails and the commit is aborted.

---

## Reference

- Husky: [typicode.github.io/husky](https://typicode.github.io/husky/)  
- Git hooks (including `commit-msg`): [Git book — hooks](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Customizing-Git-Git-Hooks)
